summary: Describes how version 2 of the Internet network management framework can live alongside the original SNMPv1 framework. It addresses how the two can work together during the transition. It was replaced by RFC 2576.

eli5.summary: When a new language comes along, people who speak the old one still need to talk to people who speak the new one. This note explains how to make both work together.

subtitle: How to manage networks during the transition from SNMPv1 to SNMPv2.

tldr.problem: SNMPv2 improved on SNMPv1 with better security and richer information descriptions, but both versions exist simultaneously in networks. There is no clear migration path between them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 coexist: MIB modules can be updated with mechanical conversion rules; proxy agents can translate between the two versions; and bilingual managers can use either protocol.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can gradually migrate from SNMPv1 to SNMPv2 without forklift upgrades, and devices using different versions can interoperate. RFC 2576 later updated this approach.

facts.label: Key improvement
facts.value: Better error reporting and richer object descriptions

today: RFC 1908 is a Draft Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 2576, which provides an updated approach to SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 coexistence. However, SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 coexistence remains common in large networks, and the principles in this document continue to guide deployments.

sections.title: Two Versions, One Network
sections.content:
SNMPv1 is the original Internet network management protocol. SNMPv2 improved it with clearer syntax, better error reporting, and richer descriptions of managed objects. However, SNMPv2 does not automatically replace SNMPv1 in deployed networks.

This document addresses the practical problem: networks contain both old SNMPv1 devices and new SNMPv2-capable devices. Managers need to query both kinds. Objects defined for SNMPv1 need to work with SNMPv2. The transition must be gradual, and both protocols must coexist during the migration period.
sections.eli5: When a network speaks two languages, both must work, and people fluent in both are needed to translate.

sections.title: Updating MIBs for SNMPv2
sections.content:
MIB modules written for SNMPv1 can be updated to SNMPv2 format through mechanical conversion. Key changes include replacing imports from the old SMI with SNMPv2-SMI, changing data types (Counter becomes Counter32, Gauge becomes Gauge32, plain INTEGER becomes Integer32), replacing ACCESS clauses with MAX-ACCESS clauses, converting MANDATORY status to CURRENT and OPTIONAL to OBSOLETE, and removing hyphens from names.

Importantly, this conversion does not require deprecating objects: the semantics of an object should only trigger deprecation if they truly change. New macros like MODULE-IDENTITY must be added, and TRAP-TYPE definitions must be converted to NOTIFICATION-TYPE. These rules allow old MIB objects to continue working while improving their description format.
sections.eli5: Old management instructions can be rewritten to follow new rules without breaking how they work.

sections.title: Proxy Agents and Bilingual Managers
sections.content:
A proxy agent sits between SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 worlds and translates between them. When an SNMPv2 manager sends a query to an SNMPv1 device, the proxy translates the request, forwards it, and translates the response back. Similarly, an SNMPv1 manager can query SNMPv2 devices through a proxy. This allows mixed networks to operate without requiring all devices to upgrade simultaneously.

A bilingual manager is an SNMPv2 management station that understands both protocols and can directly query SNMPv1 devices, translating internally as needed. This eliminates the need for a separate proxy and simplifies network architecture during migration.
sections.eli5: A translator can stand between old and new devices, or a smart manager can speak both languages directly.

sections.title: Compliance and Capability Statements
sections.content:
SNMPv2 introduces formal compliance and capability statements. When converting a standard MIB module, the document should include a MODULE-COMPLIANCE macro describing what conforming agents must implement. For describing an agent's actual capabilities (which may be a subset of a full implementation), an AGENT-CAPABILITIES macro replaces the earlier MODULE-CONFORMANCE approach from SNMPv1.

These formal statements help both operators and developers understand what to expect from a device: what is mandatory, what is optional, and what is obsolete. Conversion of these statements from SNMPv1 format requires adding status values and noting changes in the CREATION-REQUIRES clause semantics.
sections.eli5: New labels clearly say what a device must do, what it can do, and what it no longer does.
